title: Akple
localName: Akple — the Ewe answer to banku
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: Half a cup of cassava dough to a cup of corn dough, cooked ten to fifteen minutes until it forms a solid mass and no longer looks wet — and it is unfermented.
longDesc: Akple is the Ewe counterpart to banku and the surprise is that it is not fermented. The author states it plainly: it is her understanding that akple is made from unfermented corn dough. A cup of white cornmeal is blended finer, mixed with a teaspoon of corn starch and half a cup of water to make the corn dough; half a cup of drained cassava dough is blended with water; the two are mixed in a saucepan with half a cup of water and a little salt, then cooked over medium heat with another half cup added all at once and stirred until it forms a solid mass. Shaped by shaking it in a wetted calabash.
ingredients: 1 cup corn dough — see the method
1 cup white cornmeal, blended finer (optional step)
1 tsp corn starch (optional, for a smoother dough)
1/2 cup water, for mixing the cornmeal
1/2 cup water, for combining the doughs
Another 1/2 cup water, added during cooking
steps: To make the corn dough: blend a cup of white cornmeal a little finer, mix it in a bowl with a teaspoon of corn starch, then mix in half a cup of water.
To make the cassava dough: add a cup of water to a blender and blend the drained cassava to a dough or paste.
Mix the two doughs in a saucepan with half a cup of water to a smooth creamy mixture, and add a little salt. A heavy wooden spoon or stick works well.
Put the mixture on a medium heat and stir as it heats, adding another half cup of water all at once.
Continue stirring until it forms a solid mass, about 10 to 15 minutes.
Do not allow the dough to become lumpy or scorch on the bottom. Turn it as you stir.
When the mixture becomes fairly solid and no longer looks wet, wet a calabash or bowl thoroughly.
Put a spoonful of dough into the calabash and shake it vigorously, rolling the dough inside into a circle or oval.
chefTips: It is unfermented, and this is the key point. The author says so directly, which makes akple much quicker than banku — no days of souring, just dough and heat.
Solid mass and no longer looking wet is the doneness cue, at ten to fifteen minutes. That is the whole test.
The second half cup of water goes in ALL AT ONCE during cooking, not gradually. That is her instruction and it matters for the texture.
Turn it as you stir and watch the bottom. Lumpy or scorched are the two failure modes and both are irreversible.
The shaping is done by shaking a wetted calabash, not by hand — the dough rolls itself into a circle or oval inside the bowl.
One part cassava dough to two parts corn dough. The cassava is what gives akple its stretch.
Originally eaten mainly with fetri ma or fetri detsi, her own note, but it goes with fried fish and pepper sauce or shito, or palaver sauce.
commonMistakes: Fermenting the corn dough, which would make it banku.
Adding the second water gradually rather than all at once.
Shaping by hand rather than in a wetted calabash.
sources: Adapted from 'Recipe #93: Akple (corn and cassava dough)', betumiblog.blogspot.com, Thursday 21 July 2011. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Posted by Fran at 5:54 PM'. Post labels as printed: akple, banku, cassava dough, manioc dough. NO YIELD is printed.
COMMUNITY, from the post, verbatim: 'A photo at that previous blog posting shows the Ewe answer to banku: akple.'

Ingredients as printed, TWO-PASS: '1/2 cup of cassava dough'; '1 cup of corn dough'; 'a little salt (I used ~1/4 teaspoon)'; '1/2 cup of water' for mixing, then 'another half cup of water' during cooking. Her corn dough instruction, verbatim: 'I put a cup of white Indian Head cornmeal in a blender to make it a little finer (optional), then mixed it in a bowl with a teaspoon of cornstarch (also optional) to make a slightly smoother dough, then mixed 1/2 cup of water into it.' NOTE: the corn dough IS the cornmeal plus water, so the cup of cornmeal is not a separate ingredient from the cup of corn dough — one fetch listed both, which double-counts.

METHOD, quoted and TWO-PASS: 'I added a cup of water to a blender, and blended the cassava to a dough/paste.' Then: 'Mix together the 2 doughs in a saucepan with a half cup of water to get a smooth creamy mixture, and add a little salt... A nice heavy wooden spoon or stick works well.' Then: 'Put the mixture on the stove on a medium heat and stir it as it heats, adding another half cup of water all at once and continue stirring until it forms a solid mass (about 10-15 minutes). Do not allow the dough to become lumpy or scorch on the bottom. Turn it as you stir.' Then the shaping: 'When the mixture becomes fairly solid and no longer "wet" looking, take a calabash (or bowl), wet it thoroughly and put a spoonful of the dough into the calabash, shaking it vigorously and rolling the dough inside into a circle or oval shape.'

FERMENTATION STATUS, verbatim and TWO-PASS, and the reason this entry needs no fermentation cue: 'It is my understanding that akple is made from unfermented corn dough.' There is no fermentation instruction and no souring cue anywhere in the post. It is plain cornmeal, starch and water, mixed raw. Note the author's own hedge — 'It is my understanding' — which is recorded rather than firmed up.

THE ONLY TIMED WAITING STEP is the cassava drain, which belongs to the prerequisite recipe: this post says 'After 3 days, you will have a dry, tightly pressed together clump of cassava', while the prerequisite post says 2-3 days of weighted draining. NEITHER CALLS THIS FERMENTING and neither gives a smell or sour cue. See GHA043.
THE DONENESS CUE this recipe does have is for cooking rather than fermenting: 'solid mass', 'no longer "wet" looking', about 10-15 minutes.
SERVING, as printed: 'Originally, akple was eaten mainly with fetri ma or fetri detsi, but now it goes well with other dishes, such as fried fish with pepper sauce or shito, or palaver sauce.'

A COMPOSITION QUESTION LEFT OPEN: this post is tagged 'banku' as well as 'akple', and it combines corn and cassava dough — whereas her banku recipe at GHA041 uses cornmeal only. The Ivorian banku study and the FAO bulletin both describe banku as a corn-and-cassava product. So the corn-versus-corn-and-cassava distinction between banku and akple is NOT settled by these sources, and the fermented-versus-unfermented distinction may be the more reliable one.

NO ENDPOINT WAS FOUND ANYWHERE for akple as a fermented product, which is consistent with the author's statement that it is not fermented. The research literature consulted gives no akple fermentation data at all.

NO TEACHER IS NAMED. The post opens by recapping the cassava dough post: 'In July I discussed cassava (yucca, manioc) dough, and began describing how to make it--at least as far as grating the peeled cassava and pressing it to drain it for 2 or 3 days. Today's post follows up on that.'
storage: Same day. It firms as it cools.
healthBenefits: Cassava and maize together give a fuller amino acid profile than either alone.
No fermentation means no acidity, which suits sensitive stomachs.
Minimal salt — about a quarter teaspoon for two servings.
culturalNote: Akple is the Volta Region's swallow and Ewe cooks will tell you it is not banku, whatever it looks like in the bowl. If the fermented-versus-unfermented distinction holds, they are right in a way that goes beyond regional pride: one is a soured dough and the other is not, and they taste quite different as a result.
